title: Don't call the scriptures false
hook: don't call the Vedas and the Semitic books false; false is the one who doesn't reflect (Prabhati, Kabir, ang 1350)
tomorrow: I am the worst of all

segments.voice: Yesterday, Brahmin: Kabir asked a learned man how he was born, and your line was born the same way. Today Kabir turns from birth to books.

Two shelves. On one, the Vedas, the old hymns of the Hindu tradition. On the other, the Kateb, Kabir's word for the books of the Muslim neighbors, the Qur'an among them. A weaver who has just told a learned man that birth makes no one higher might be expected to sweep both shelves onto the floor. If caste doesn't count, maybe the books don't either. That's not what he does. In Raag Prabhati, Kabir draws a line in a very different place.
screen: `TWO SHELVES.` → `THE VEDAS AND THE KATEB.` → `A LINE IN A DIFFERENT PLACE.`

segments.voice: Kabir's hymns in Raag Prabhati sit close together on the page. One opens wide: first, God made the light, and from that one light the whole creation came. So who is good and who is bad? Then, in a neighboring hymn, comes the line in today's title. Don't say the Vedas and the Kateb are false. False is the one who doesn't reflect. That moves the problem. The danger isn't sitting on the shelf. It's sitting in the reader. A book can be read with care or with no thought at all; someone can carry a holy text everywhere and never once stop to think about what it asks. Kabir points there, not at the pages. And he isn't saying all books say the same thing, or asking anyone to give up their own. He's naming a habit: dismissing a scripture you haven't sat with, or reciting your own without letting it reach you. Both skip the same step. The word in the line is bichar: to reflect, to think something through. Sikh teachers say the Guru's word asks to be understood, not only recited. Read that way, Kabir's line asks the same of every reader, whatever shelf they read from: sit with a line before calling a book empty, and let your own book reach you before calling it full.
screen: `FROM ONE LIGHT, THE WHOLE CREATION.` · `FALSE IS THE ONE WHO DOESN'T REFLECT.` · `THE DANGER SITS IN THE READER.` · `BICHAR: THINK IT THROUGH.` · then, large: `REFLECT, DON'T DISMISS.`

segments.voice: Bring one line of any scripture to mind, your own, a neighbor's, one you've only heard quoted, or today's: false is the one who doesn't reflect. Say it slowly inside and ask what it is asking of you, without arguing and without rushing to agree, turning it like a stone in your hand. If you pray, you can say Waheguru before and after.
Bichar. To reflect, to think something through: Kabir's word for the one thing a reader of any scripture owes it before calling it empty.
Your line: reflect, don't dismiss. The danger sits in the reader, not on the shelf. Day seven hundred fifty-three, done.

screen: `DAY 753 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: I AM THE WORST OF ALL.`

howItsDone: Sikhs sing this Prabhati hymn of Kabir in kirtan, and Sikh teachers use its line on the Vedas and the Kateb to call listeners to reflect on scripture rather than dismiss anyone's.

chat.says: Did Kabir say other people's holy books were false?
options: No: don't call the Vedas or Kateb false; false is the one who doesn't reflect.
Yes: he said every book was false, and only singing God's name was true.
No: he said books don't matter either way, so there's no need to think about them.

Editor: the 'one light' opening (Aval Allah noor upaaiaa, Ang 1349) and the Bed/Kateb line (Ang 1350) are separate Prabhati hymns; teach, myth and trapdoor no longer present them as one hymn. Dropped 'Punjabi' as the line's language.

Audit: Kateb gloss tightened to 'Kabir's word for the books of the Muslim neighbors, the Qur'an among them' (Kateb is usually read as the Semitic scriptures, so not the Qur'an alone); the teach's closing 'before you call a book empty...' recast as what the line asks, not a direct instruction to the listener.
